title: What Koreans Are Obsessed With Right Now: A Salaryman's Seoul Snapshot

📅 Updated 2026.09.18
Key takeaways
  • As of September 2026, Koreans are deeply integrating AI into daily life for hyper-personalized experiences.
  • There's a strong push towards niche hobbies and micro-communities for personal fulfillment, a contrast to fast-paced work.
  • A 'Newtro' wave is reshaping consumption, blending modern tech with retro aesthetics for unique experiences.
👤 This is for readers who are curious about what's genuinely popular and shaping daily life in Seoul, explained by a local insider.

Lately in Korea, the pace of change feels faster than ever, even for us locals. If you're wondering what Koreans are obsessed with right now, as of September 17, 2026, it's a fascinating mix of cutting-edge tech, personal well-being, and a deep dive into nostalgia. Forget just K-Pop and K-dramas; the real trends are happening in our daily lives, from how we work and commute to how we spend our precious free time. It's about finding efficiency, connection, and a bit of soul in this bustling city.

The AI Everywhere Revolution: Smarter Living, Smarter Working

Honestly, the biggest thing shaping what Koreans are obsessed with right now is the quiet, pervasive integration of artificial intelligence into almost everything. It’s not just a Silicon Valley buzzword here; AI is deeply woven into our daily apps and services, making life hyper-personalized and ridiculously efficient. Think beyond just chatbots. We’re talking about AI-powered recommendations that predict your next favorite café order with unnerving accuracy, or generative AI tools that practically write your emails for you at work.

In my office, for instance, everyone relies on a specialized AI assistant service, let’s call it ‘WorkBrain’, which integrates with our company’s internal systems. It drafts basic reports, summarizes long meeting transcripts, and even helps schedule complex cross-departmental calls, avoiding the usual nunchi (the art of reading the room) pitfalls of finding an open slot. It costs my company roughly 20,000 won per employee per month (~$15 USD), but the time savings are huge. My commute planner app, ‘SeoulFlow’, now uses real-time AI to suggest not just the fastest subway route, but also the least crowded car on the train, predicting passenger flow based on historical data and current events. It’s incredibly precise. The first time it told me to get in the second car from the front for a smoother transfer, I was skeptical, but it was perfectly accurate. It’s convenience taken to the extreme, making our already palli-palli (hurry-hurry, do-it-now mindset) even faster.

Point: It's undeniably convenient and boosts productivity, but sometimes I miss the serendipity of discovery when an algorithm knows you better than you know yourself.

Finding Zen in the Urban Jungle: Niche Hobbies and Micro-Communities

Despite the AI-driven rush, there's a strong counter-current here in Seoul: a deep desire for balance and personal fulfillment through highly specific hobbies and tight-knit micro-communities. This is another major answer to what Koreans are obsessed with right now. It's part of the 'hobby-conomy,' where people are investing serious time and money into their passions, often seeking out sohwakhaeng (small, definite happiness) away from the pressures of work. This isn't just about general fitness; it's about hyper-niche activities.

For example, urban bouldering has absolutely exploded. You see new bouldering gyms popping up in basements and renovated warehouses all over Gangnam and Hongdae. A monthly membership typically runs about 80,000 to 100,000 won (~$60-75 USD), and people are obsessed with improving their technique and sharing tips. I tried it once with a colleague, and while my hands hated me for a week, the sense of community was palpable. People connect through apps like ‘MeetUpKorea’ (a popular local version of Meetup.com) or even just KakaoTalk chat groups dedicated to specific interests – think ‘Seoul Analog Film Photography Walks,’ ‘Urban Sketching in Ikseon-dong,’ or ‘Home Bar Mixology Enthusiasts.’ These groups are often small, exclusive, and foster incredibly strong bonds, providing a sense of belonging that's hard to find in a large, anonymous city. My coworker, Manager Kim, is completely engrossed in 'micro-gardening' – cultivating tiny, elaborate terrariums for her desk. She even joined an online community for it, exchanging rare moss and miniature succulents.

Point: It’s a healthy escape from work life, but the pressure to be 'good' at your hobby and participate in the community can sometimes feel like another job.

The Retro-Fusion Craze: Nostalgia with a Modern Twist

Another huge cultural wave that encapsulates what Koreans are obsessed with right now is 'Newtro' (new + retro) – a fascinating blend of nostalgia and modern sensibilities. It's not just about bringing back old trends; it's about reinterpreting the past with contemporary aesthetics, technology, and a fresh perspective. Think old-school charm filtered through a minimalist, Instagram-ready lens.

Walk through neighborhoods like Ikseon-dong or Euljiro, and you'll see this trend everywhere. We have LP (long-play record) cafes that look straight out of the 1980s, complete with worn leather sofas and vintage turntables, but you order your artisanal coffee (an 8,000 won, or ~$6 USD, experience) using a QR code on your smartphone. Fashion sees a lot of this too: vintage tracksuits paired with cutting-edge sneakers, or classic hanbok (traditional Korean dress) patterns reimagined in modern, streetwear silhouettes. Even traditional Korean snacks, like old-school rice crackers or dalgona (honeycomb candy), are being repackaged in sleek, premium designs at convenience stores and department stores. The first time I visited a Newtro cafe, I felt like I'd stepped onto a movie set – everything was perfectly curated to evoke a bygone era, yet the Wi-Fi was blazing fast and the baristas were rocking smartwatches. It’s about experiencing the 'vibe' of the past without giving up modern comforts. This 'Newstalgia' also extends to analog tech, with instant cameras and portable CD players making a surprising comeback, sometimes even costing more than their digital counterparts simply for the aesthetic.

Point: It’s a fun, aesthetic trend that offers a pleasant escape, but it sometimes feels a bit manufactured, prioritizing style over genuine historical depth.

Conscious Consumption: Upcycling and Second-Hand Surges

Finally, what Koreans are obsessed with right now, particularly among younger generations but increasingly with everyone, is conscious consumption. Driven by both growing environmental awareness and the practicalities of a fluctuating economy, there's been a massive surge in upcycling, second-hand markets, and supporting sustainable brands. It's a shift from 'buy new, discard fast' to 'reuse, repurpose, rethink.'

The dominant force here is Karrot Market (also known as Daangn Market), the local second-hand app. If you live in Korea, you will use Karrot. It's like a hyper-local Craigslist mixed with a friendly neighborhood forum. I've sold everything from an old desk for 50,000 won (~$38 USD) to a barely-used blender, and bought a vintage lamp for a fraction of its new price. My colleagues constantly share their latest Karrot finds in our group chat. Beyond just selling used items, upcycling brands are gaining serious traction. You see fashion labels creating bags from discarded banners, or furniture makers transforming industrial waste into chic home decor. There are even dedicated zero-waste stores popping up, encouraging people to bring their own containers for groceries and daily essentials. This trend highlights a growing awareness of jeong (a deep, sticky sense of attachment between people or things) extending to our possessions and the environment. It’s practical, saves money, and feels good.

Point: It’s a truly positive trend that's both economically smart and environmentally responsible, though some still quietly hold a stigma against used items.

A. Newtro is a portmanteau of 'new' and 'retro,' describing a trend in Korea where vintage aesthetics and cultural elements are reinterpreted and blended with modern design, technology, and sensibilities, creating a fresh take on nostalgia.

Q. How is AI impacting daily life for Koreans?

A. AI is deeply integrated into daily life for Koreans, moving beyond simple chatbots to provide hyper-personalized recommendations in apps, optimize commutes with real-time data, and streamline work tasks like report drafting and scheduling through advanced AI assistant services.

Q. What are some popular niche hobbies in Seoul right now?

A. Popular niche hobbies in Seoul as of 2026 include urban bouldering, micro-gardening (terrariums), analog film photography walks, urban sketching, and home bar mixology, often pursued within dedicated online or offline micro-communities.

Q. What is Karrot Market and why is it popular in Korea?

A. Karrot Market (Daangn Market) is a hyper-local second-hand app popular in Korea that allows users to easily buy and sell used goods within their immediate neighborhood. It's popular due to its convenience, affordability, and the sense of local community it fosters for conscious consumption.

Q. Are Koreans still interested in K-Pop and K-dramas?

A. While K-Pop and K-dramas remain globally popular and a significant part of Korean culture, the blog post focuses on deeper, everyday lifestyle and consumption trends that also define what Koreans are obsessed with right now, beyond just entertainment.

한국인들이 지금 무엇에 열광하는가: 한 직장인의 서울 스냅샷

최근 한국에서는 우리 현지인들에게도 변화의 속도가 그 어느 때보다 빠르게 느껴집니다. 2026년 9월 17일 현재 한국인들이 무엇에 열광하는지 궁금하시다면, 그것은 최첨단 기술, 개인의 웰빙, 그리고 향수에 대한 깊은 탐구가 흥미롭게 혼합된 것입니다. K-Pop과 K-드라마는 잊으세요. 진정한 트렌드는 우리가 일하고 통근하는 방식부터 소중한 자유 시간을 보내는 방식에 이르기까지 우리의 일상생활에서 일어나고 있습니다. 이 번잡한 도시에서 효율성, 연결성, 그리고 약간의 영혼을 찾는 것이 중요합니다.

## 어디에나 있는 AI 혁명: 더 스마트한 삶, 더 스마트한 업무

솔직히, 한국인들이 지금 열광하는 것을 형성하는 가장 큰 것은 인공지능이 거의 모든 것에 조용하고 광범위하게 통합되는 것입니다. 이곳에서는 실리콘밸리의 유행어가 아닙니다. AI는 우리의 일상 앱과 서비스에 깊이 스며들어 삶을 초개인화하고 터무니없이 효율적으로 만듭니다. 챗봇 그 이상을 생각해보세요. 우리는 당신이 다음에 가장 좋아하는 카페 주문을 소름 끼치도록 정확하게 예측하는 AI 기반 추천이나, 직장에서 당신의 이메일을 사실상 대신 써주는 생성형 AI 도구에 대해 이야기하고 있습니다.

예를 들어, 제 사무실에서는 모든 사람이 회사 내부 시스템과 통합되는 전문 AI 비서 서비스, 즉 '워크브레인'에 의존합니다. 이 서비스는 기본적인 보고서를 작성하고, 긴 회의록을 요약하며, 심지어 복잡한 부서 간 통화를 예약하는 데 도움을 주어, 빈 시간을 찾는 데 따르는 일반적인 눈치(상황을 읽는 기술)의 함정을 피합니다. 제 회사에서는 직원 1인당 월 약 20,000원(~$15 USD)이 들지만, 시간 절약 효과는 엄청납니다. 제 통근 계획 앱인 '서울플로우'는 이제 실시간 AI를 사용하여 가장 빠른 지하철 노선뿐만 아니라, 과거 데이터와 현재 사건을 기반으로 승객 흐름을 예측하여 열차에서 가장 붐비지 않는 칸까지 제안합니다. 믿을 수 없을 정도로 정확합니다. 처음으로 더 원활한 환승을 위해 앞에서 두 번째 칸에 타라고 했을 때 저는 회의적이었지만, 완벽하게 정확했습니다. 이것은 극단적인 편리함으로, 우리의 이미 빨리빨리(서둘러, 지금 당장 해) 사고방식을 더욱 빠르게 만듭니다.

> 요점: 의심할 여지 없이 편리하고 생산성을 높이지만, 때로는 알고리즘이 나 자신보다 나를 더 잘 알 때 발견의 우연성을 놓치기도 합니다.

## 도시 정글에서 선(禪) 찾기: 틈새 취미와 마이크로 커뮤니티

AI 중심의 서두름에도 불구하고, 서울에는 강한 역류가 있습니다. 바로 매우 구체적인 취미와 긴밀한 마이크로 커뮤니티를 통해 균형과 개인적인 성취를 찾고자 하는 깊은 열망입니다. 이것은 한국인들이 지금 열광하는 것에 대한 또 다른 중요한 답변입니다. 이것은 사람들이 직장의 압력에서 벗어나 소확행(작지만 확실한 행복)을 추구하며 자신의 열정에 진지한 시간과 돈을 투자하는 '취미 경제'의 일부입니다. 이것은 단순히 일반적인 피트니스에 관한 것이 아니라, 초틈새 활동에 관한 것입니다.

예를 들어, 도시 볼더링은 완전히 폭발적으로 인기를 얻었습니다. 강남과 홍대 전역의 지하와 개조된 창고에서 새로운 볼더링 체육관이 계속 생겨나는 것을 볼 수 있습니다. 월 회비는 보통 80,000원에서 100,000원(~$60-75 USD) 정도이며, 사람들은 기술을 향상시키고 팁을 공유하는 데 열광합니다. 저는 동료와 함께 한 번 시도해 보았는데, 일주일 동안 손이 아팠지만, 공동체 의식은 분명했습니다. 사람들은 'MeetUpKorea'(Meetup.com의 인기 있는 현지 버전)와 같은 앱이나 특정 관심사에 전념하는 카카오톡 채팅 그룹을 통해 연결됩니다. 예를 들어 '서울 아날로그 필름 사진 산책', '익선동 도시 스케치', '홈 바 믹솔로지 애호가' 등이 있습니다. 이러한 그룹은 종종 작고 배타적이며, 매우 강력한 유대감을 형성하여 크고 익명의 도시에서 찾기 어려운 소속감을 제공합니다. 제 동료인 김 부장님은 '마이크로 가드닝'에 완전히 몰두해 있습니다. 그녀의 책상을 위한 작고 정교한 테라리움을 가꾸는 것입니다. 그녀는 심지어 온라인 커뮤니티에 가입하여 희귀한 이끼와 미니어처 다육식물을 교환하기도 합니다.

> 요점: 직장 생활에서 벗어나는 건강한 탈출구이지만, 취미에 '능숙해야 한다'는 압박감과 커뮤니티에 참여해야 한다는 부담감이 때로는 또 다른 일처럼 느껴질 수 있습니다.

## 레트로 퓨전 열풍: 현대적인 감각이 가미된 향수

한국인들이 지금 열광하는 것을 아우르는 또 다른 거대한 문화적 흐름은 '뉴트로'(new + retro)입니다. 향수와 현대적인 감각이 매혹적으로 혼합된 것입니다. 단순히 오래된 트렌드를 되살리는 것이 아니라, 현대적인 미학, 기술, 그리고 신선한 관점으로 과거를 재해석하는 것입니다. 미니멀하고 인스타그램에 올리기 좋은 렌즈를 통해 걸러진 옛날의 매력을 생각해보세요.

익선동이나 을지로와 같은 동네를 걸어보면 이 트렌드를 어디에서나 볼 수 있습니다. 낡은 가죽 소파와 빈티지 턴테이블을 갖춘 1980년대에서 바로 나온 듯한 LP(장시간 재생 레코드) 카페가 있지만, 스마트폰의 QR 코드를 사용하여 장인 정신이 깃든 커피(8,000원, 약 $6 USD 경험)를 주문합니다. 패션에서도 이런 경향이 많이 보입니다. 빈티지 트레이닝복과 최첨단 운동화를 매치하거나, 전통 한복 패턴을 현대적인 스트리트웨어 실루엣으로 재해석하는 식입니다. 심지어 옛날 쌀과자나 달고나와 같은 전통 한국 간식도 편의점과 백화점에서 세련되고 고급스러운 디자인으로 재포장되고 있습니다. 제가 뉴트로 카페를 처음 방문했을 때, 영화 세트장에 들어선 것 같은 느낌이 들었습니다. 모든 것이 지나간 시대를 연상시키도록 완벽하게 큐레이션되어 있었지만, Wi-Fi는 엄청나게 빨랐고 바리스타들은 스마트워치를 착용하고 있었습니다. 이것은 현대적인 편안함을 포기하지 않고 과거의 '분위기'를 경험하는 것입니다. 이러한 '뉴스타일'은 아날로그 기술에도 확장되어, 즉석 카메라와 휴대용 CD 플레이어가 놀랍게도 다시 인기를 얻고 있으며, 때로는 단순히 미학적인 이유로 디지털 제품보다 더 비싸기도 합니다.

> 요점: 즐겁고 미학적인 트렌드로 즐거운 탈출구를 제공하지만, 때로는 진정한 역사적 깊이보다 스타일을 우선시하여 다소 인위적으로 느껴지기도 합니다.

## 의식 있는 소비: 업사이클링과 중고품 급증

마지막으로, 한국인들이 지금 열광하는 것, 특히 젊은 세대 사이에서 그리고 점점 더 모든 사람들에게 퍼지고 있는 것은 의식 있는 소비입니다. 환경 의식의 성장과 변동하는 경제의 실용성이라는 두 가지 요인에 의해 주도되어, 업사이클링, 중고 시장, 그리고 지속 가능한 브랜드 지원이 엄청나게 증가했습니다. 이것은 '새것을 사고 빨리 버리는' 것에서 '재사용하고, 용도를 변경하고, 다시 생각하는' 것으로의 전환입니다.

여기서 지배적인 힘은 지역 중고 앱인 당근마켓(Karrot Market)입니다. 한국에 살고 있다면 당근마켓을 *사용하게 될 것입니다*. 이것은 초지역적인 크레이그리스트와 친근한 동네 포럼이 혼합된 것과 같습니다. 저는 50,000원(~$38 USD)짜리 낡은 책상부터 거의 사용하지 않은 믹서기까지 모든 것을 팔았고, 새 가격의 일부만 주고 빈티지 램프를 샀습니다. 제 동료들은 그룹 채팅에서 최신 당근마켓 발견품을 끊임없이 공유합니다. 단순히 중고품을 판매하는 것을 넘어, 업사이클링 브랜드가 진지한 인기를 얻고 있습니다. 버려진 현수막으로 가방을 만드는 패션 브랜드나 산업 폐기물을 세련된 가정용 장식품으로 바꾸는 가구 제조업체를 볼 수 있습니다. 심지어 제로 웨이스트 상점도 생겨나 사람들이 식료품과 일상 필수품을 위해 자신의 용기를 가져오도록 장려하고 있습니다. 이러한 트렌드는 우리의 소유물과 환경으로 확장되는 정(사람이나 사물 사이의 깊고 끈끈한 애착)에 대한 인식이 커지고 있음을 보여줍니다. 실용적이고, 돈을 절약하며, 기분 좋은 일입니다.

> 요점: 경제적으로 현명하고 환경적으로 책임감 있는 진정으로 긍정적인 트렌드이지만, 일부는 여전히 중고품에 대한 낙인을 조용히 가지고 있습니다.
content_raw:
Lately in Korea, the pace of change feels faster than ever, even for us locals. If you're wondering what Koreans are obsessed with right now, as of September 17, 2026, it's a fascinating mix of cutting-edge tech, personal well-being, and a deep dive into nostalgia. Forget just K-Pop and K-dramas; the real trends are happening in our daily lives, from how we work and commute to how we spend our precious free time. It's about finding efficiency, connection, and a bit of soul in this bustling city.

## The AI Everywhere Revolution: Smarter Living, Smarter Working

Honestly, the biggest thing shaping what Koreans are obsessed with right now is the quiet, pervasive integration of artificial intelligence into almost everything. It’s not just a Silicon Valley buzzword here; AI is deeply woven into our daily apps and services, making life hyper-personalized and ridiculously efficient. Think beyond just chatbots. We’re talking about AI-powered recommendations that predict your next favorite café order with unnerving accuracy, or generative AI tools that practically write your emails for you at work.

In my office, for instance, everyone relies on a specialized AI assistant service, let’s call it ‘WorkBrain’, which integrates with our company’s internal systems. It drafts basic reports, summarizes long meeting transcripts, and even helps schedule complex cross-departmental calls, avoiding the usual nunchi (the art of reading the room) pitfalls of finding an open slot. It costs my company roughly 20,000 won per employee per month (~$15 USD), but the time savings are huge. My commute planner app, ‘SeoulFlow’, now uses real-time AI to suggest not just the fastest subway route, but also the least crowded car on the train, predicting passenger flow based on historical data and current events. It’s incredibly precise. The first time it told me to get in the second car from the front for a smoother transfer, I was skeptical, but it was perfectly accurate. It’s convenience taken to the extreme, making our already palli-palli (hurry-hurry, do-it-now mindset) even faster.

> Point: It's undeniably convenient and boosts productivity, but sometimes I miss the serendipity of discovery when an algorithm knows you better than you know yourself.

## Finding Zen in the Urban Jungle: Niche Hobbies and Micro-Communities

Despite the AI-driven rush, there's a strong counter-current here in Seoul: a deep desire for balance and personal fulfillment through highly specific hobbies and tight-knit micro-communities. This is another major answer to what Koreans are obsessed with right now. It's part of the 'hobby-conomy,' where people are investing serious time and money into their passions, often seeking out sohwakhaeng (small, definite happiness) away from the pressures of work. This isn't just about general fitness; it's about hyper-niche activities.

For example, urban bouldering has absolutely exploded. You see new bouldering gyms popping up in basements and renovated warehouses all over Gangnam and Hongdae. A monthly membership typically runs about 80,000 to 100,000 won (~$60-75 USD), and people are obsessed with improving their technique and sharing tips. I tried it once with a colleague, and while my hands hated me for a week, the sense of community was palpable. People connect through apps like ‘MeetUpKorea’ (a popular local version of Meetup.com) or even just KakaoTalk chat groups dedicated to specific interests – think ‘Seoul Analog Film Photography Walks,’ ‘Urban Sketching in Ikseon-dong,’ or ‘Home Bar Mixology Enthusiasts.’ These groups are often small, exclusive, and foster incredibly strong bonds, providing a sense of belonging that's hard to find in a large, anonymous city. My coworker, Manager Kim, is completely engrossed in 'micro-gardening' – cultivating tiny, elaborate terrariums for her desk. She even joined an online community for it, exchanging rare moss and miniature succulents.

> Point: It’s a healthy escape from work life, but the pressure to be 'good' at your hobby and participate in the community can sometimes feel like another job.

## The Retro-Fusion Craze: Nostalgia with a Modern Twist

Another huge cultural wave that encapsulates what Koreans are obsessed with right now is 'Newtro' (new + retro) – a fascinating blend of nostalgia and modern sensibilities. It's not just about bringing back old trends; it's about reinterpreting the past with contemporary aesthetics, technology, and a fresh perspective. Think old-school charm filtered through a minimalist, Instagram-ready lens.

Walk through neighborhoods like Ikseon-dong or Euljiro, and you'll see this trend everywhere. We have LP (long-play record) cafes that look straight out of the 1980s, complete with worn leather sofas and vintage turntables, but you order your artisanal coffee (an 8,000 won, or ~$6 USD, experience) using a QR code on your smartphone. Fashion sees a lot of this too: vintage tracksuits paired with cutting-edge sneakers, or classic hanbok (traditional Korean dress) patterns reimagined in modern, streetwear silhouettes. Even traditional Korean snacks, like old-school rice crackers or dalgona (honeycomb candy), are being repackaged in sleek, premium designs at convenience stores and department stores. The first time I visited a Newtro cafe, I felt like I'd stepped onto a movie set – everything was perfectly curated to evoke a bygone era, yet the Wi-Fi was blazing fast and the baristas were rocking smartwatches. It’s about experiencing the 'vibe' of the past without giving up modern comforts. This 'Newstalgia' also extends to analog tech, with instant cameras and portable CD players making a surprising comeback, sometimes even costing more than their digital counterparts simply for the aesthetic.

> Point: It’s a fun, aesthetic trend that offers a pleasant escape, but it sometimes feels a bit manufactured, prioritizing style over genuine historical depth.

## Conscious Consumption: Upcycling and Second-Hand Surges

Finally, what Koreans are obsessed with right now, particularly among younger generations but increasingly with everyone, is conscious consumption. Driven by both growing environmental awareness and the practicalities of a fluctuating economy, there's been a massive surge in upcycling, second-hand markets, and supporting sustainable brands. It's a shift from 'buy new, discard fast' to 'reuse, repurpose, rethink.'

The dominant force here is Karrot Market (also known as Daangn Market), the local second-hand app. If you live in Korea, you will use Karrot. It's like a hyper-local Craigslist mixed with a friendly neighborhood forum. I've sold everything from an old desk for 50,000 won (~$38 USD) to a barely-used blender, and bought a vintage lamp for a fraction of its new price. My colleagues constantly share their latest Karrot finds in our group chat. Beyond just selling used items, upcycling brands are gaining serious traction. You see fashion labels creating bags from discarded banners, or furniture makers transforming industrial waste into chic home decor. There are even dedicated zero-waste stores popping up, encouraging people to bring their own containers for groceries and daily essentials. This trend highlights a growing awareness of jeong (a deep, sticky sense of attachment between people or things) extending to our possessions and the environment. It’s practical, saves money, and feels good.

> Point: It’s a truly positive trend that's both economically smart and environmentally responsible, though some still quietly hold a stigma against used items.
